task.goal: Create an optional two-minute interaction that helps people notice overlooked textures in a public garden.
hard_constraints: Two volunteers have three weeks, weatherproof printed material and permission for a freestanding sign only.
No touching plants, collecting visitor details, power or phone requirement.
Usable from a seated position and worthwhile for someone passing quickly; pilot against a plain information sign without claiming results.
task.available_resources: Existing garden map and volunteer observation shifts.
task.expected_result: A specific low-cost interaction and pilot signals.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One View, Three Scales
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
A freestanding sign guides an optional two-minute visual search within one garden view: “Ten seconds? Find one texture you had not noticed.” The longer sequence asks visitors to look across the whole planting for a soft or jagged outline, choose one visible patch with repeated marks, then look for the smallest detail they can comfortably distinguish. Finish by returning to the whole view and noticing whether it now looks different. No approach to plants is required.

The mechanism is a deliberate change in viewing scale: successive prompts may interrupt habitual scanning and reveal texture already present. This assumes the permitted sign location offers several distinguishable textures from a seated position. Fine detail may be inaccessible to some visitors, so each step explicitly allows staying with larger patterns; the interaction does not promise equal visual access.

Two volunteers use the existing map to shortlist locations, then inspect actual views from seated height. Choose one with clear sightlines and room to stop without obstructing circulation. Print three large, high-contrast prompts on weatherproof material, with a simple diagram showing the relevant viewing direction. Keep the quick invitation prominent and the longer sequence optional. Week one covers siting and drafting, week two a full-size readability check and revision, and week three the pilot. Costs are printing and a permitted, stable sign support; no additional installation is needed.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate this sign and a plain information sign on the same support in comparable observation blocks. The comparator gives factual information about the same visible planting, with similar print size and text length. Volunteers tally anonymous passersby, stops, approximate dwell-time bands, and visible shifts between the indicated garden areas; gaze alone cannot establish noticing. During a few staffed blocks, offer an optional verbal question: “What texture, if any, stood out?” Record only aggregate counts of specific texture descriptions, without names, recordings or visitor characteristics. A small falsifying check is whether seated readers can locate the three scales at all. If they cannot, or interaction blocks produce no clearer texture descriptions than the comparator, revise or drop the sequence. Report the small pilot descriptively, without claiming effectiveness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Which Word Fits?
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
A freestanding sign presents three short pairs of contrasting texture words, such as “rippled / tangled,” “velvety / wiry,” and “layered / scattered.” Visitors silently choose which word best describes one clearly indicated garden patch. The ten-second version is one choice; the optional two-minute version asks them to find evidence for both words, then invent a better description in their head. The sign says that these are visual comparisons, not invitations to touch.

The mechanism is interpretive disagreement: choosing between imperfect labels gives visitors a reason to inspect a familiar-looking surface more carefully. Seeking evidence for the rejected word can expose overlooked variation. Unlike a factual identification exercise, there is no correct answer to reveal. Its value depends on the chosen patch supporting more than one plausible description; a visually uniform or obscured patch would make the choice arbitrary.

Using the existing map, two volunteers select a permitted sign position beside a view containing visibly contrasting textures at seated eye level. They draft everyday words and simple line illustrations so the invitation does not depend entirely on vocabulary. Large type, strong contrast and an unobstructed stopping space support seated participation. Visitors may complete everything silently, without writing, tokens or moving components. One weatherproof printed panel and stable freestanding support suffice. Across three weeks, the volunteers inspect the location, check the language and seated sightline, revise the print, and run observation shifts. Seasonal changes and unfamiliar metaphorical words remain limitations; labels must be chosen for the actual view.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot against a plain information sign describing the same patch, alternating matched observation blocks at the same location. Count anonymous passersby, stops and dwell-time bands. In a small number of staffed checks, invite visitors to name one visible feature supporting their chosen word; keep only aggregate counts, without collecting identifying information or recording speech. Include readers viewing from seated height in the prototype check. The central challenge is whether the words cause closer inspection: if people choose immediately but cannot point out any supporting feature, or describe no more texture detail than readers of the plain sign, the proposed mechanism has weak support. Also check whether either word is consistently confusing. Treat findings as local pilot signals, not demonstrated benefits.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Draw It in the Air—with Your Eyes
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
A freestanding sign invites visitors to imagine drawing one visible garden texture without moving their hands: “Ten seconds? Follow one edge with your eyes.” The optional two-minute sequence continues: trace a second edge, notice whether its imagined line would be straight, broken, curling or branching, then find a nearby texture that would need a different kind of line. Visitors finish by looking back at the original patch.

The mechanism is imagined mark-making. Translating a surface into lines may shift attention from identifying plants to noticing the structure of their edges, veins, stems and shadows. It is independently usable without drawing supplies, touching plants, power or a phone. The assumption is that visitors can distinguish sufficiently large contours from the sign. Some people find mental imagery difficult, so the wording also permits simply following an outline and comparing its shape. It remains primarily a visual experience and will have limits for visitors with low vision.

Two volunteers use the garden map and a seated-height inspection to choose a permitted position facing clear, contrasting outlines. A weatherproof panel carries three large example strokes and concise instructions; the examples explain the action without purporting to depict every plant. The sign directs attention using an unmistakable landmark already in the view. A stable freestanding support sits outside the circulation route. Preparation fits three weeks: choose the view and draft in week one, test readability and landmark clarity in week two, then revise and pilot in week three. Printing and the support are the only material needs. Avoid tiny veins or distant features that would encourage visitors to leave the accessible viewing point.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate the interaction with a plain information sign about the same garden view, using comparable time blocks and the same support. Volunteers tally passing traffic, stops and dwell-time bands anonymously. A few optional verbal checks ask visitors to identify two textures that would require different drawing strokes; record only aggregate completion counts, with no identifying details or recordings. Before the pilot, test whether seated readers can find the landmark and follow a contour without changing position. The idea is weakened if instructions repeatedly require explanation, readers cannot identify contrasting strokes, or the plain information sign elicits equally specific texture distinctions. Observe across more than one light condition because shadows may determine legibility. Report feasibility and descriptive differences only; this small pilot cannot establish a reliable effect.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Look Through the Gaps
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
A freestanding sign invites visitors to notice texture by looking at the empty spaces within a planting: “Ten seconds? Find one gap between leaves or stems. Notice its shape.” The optional two-minute interaction continues: find several neighboring gaps, notice how their spacing creates a loose or dense pattern, then look back at the plants surrounding them. Everything happens from the sign; visitors need not approach or touch plants.

The mechanism is figure–ground reversal. Attention normally falls on plants as objects; treating the background openings as the subject may expose the arrangement that makes foliage appear lacy, mesh-like or tightly packed. The change in attention, rather than a change in viewing scale or a choice of descriptive words, drives the interaction.

This requires a planting with clearly visible openings against a contrasting background from seated height. Dense foliage, poor contrast or seasonal growth could make the exercise ineffective. It is primarily visual and cannot offer equivalent access to every visitor.

Two volunteers use the existing map to shortlist permitted locations, then inspect the actual sightlines from seated height. One weatherproof panel uses large, high-contrast text, an arrow toward an existing landmark and a simple illustration of spaces between shapes. A stable freestanding support must fit the available budget or be borrowed, and leave circulation clear. Week one covers siting and drafting; week two covers a full-size readability and seated-view check; week three covers revision and observation shifts. There are no loose pieces, writing tasks or visitor records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate the interaction and a plain information sign about the same planting in comparable observation blocks on the same support. Tally anonymous passing traffic, stops and approximate dwell-time bands. During selected staffed blocks, ask an optional question: “What pattern, if any, did you notice?” Keep only aggregate counts of responses describing gaps, spacing or plant texture, without names, recordings or visitor characteristics. The smallest falsifying check is whether a seated reader can identify several visible gaps without explanation or repositioning. If that fails, reject the location. If readers notice isolated holes but cannot relate them to the surrounding texture, or responses are no more specific than with the information sign, the proposed mechanism has weak support. Report local descriptive signals only.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Look Away, Then Look Again
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
A freestanding sign offers a brief visual-memory challenge: “Ten seconds? Look at this planting, look away briefly, then look back. What detail escaped your first look?” The optional two-minute version asks visitors to study a clearly indicated patch, turn their gaze toward a printed dot on the sign, silently recall its surface pattern, then return to the patch and find something missing from their mental picture. They may repeat once, keeping their gaze shifts comfortable and their head still.

The mechanism is a gap between remembered appearance and visible detail. A planting may initially register as a general mass; attempting to recall its texture can make missing information apparent and give the second look a specific purpose. Success means discovering a previously omitted feature, rather than remembering accurately. No answer is written or submitted.

This assumes visitors can comfortably alternate their gaze between sign and planting and understand the short sequence. Visual memory varies, and some people may find the challenge frustrating. The sign therefore says that an incomplete memory is expected and that participation can end after one return look. The experience remains primarily visual.

Two volunteers use the garden map and seated-height inspections to select a clear, nearby view with visible texture and an unmistakable landmark. They produce one weatherproof panel with large text and three simple symbols: look, look away, return. The panel sits on a stable permitted freestanding support outside the circulation route. Printing and a borrowed or inexpensive support are the material needs. Within three weeks, the volunteers select the site, check a full-size prototype for readability and comprehension, revise it, and run observation shifts.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare this panel with a plain information sign about the same view, alternating comparable observation blocks. Volunteers tally anonymous passersby, stops and dwell-time bands. In a few staffed blocks, offer the same optional question under both conditions: “Did a second look reveal any texture detail you missed initially?” Retain only aggregate counts of concrete examples, with no identifying information or recordings. First conduct a small seated-position comprehension check: can readers complete the sequence without coaching? Repeated confusion, discomfort or interpreting it as a memory exam would falsify the current wording. If the sequence is understood but yields no more concrete discoveries than the plain sign, its added value remains unsupported. Dwell time alone cannot establish noticing; report the pilot descriptively without claiming effectiveness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Watch the Texture Move
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
A freestanding sign invites visitors to notice texture as something that changes: “Ten seconds? Find a patch whose pattern moves in the breeze.” The optional two-minute sequence asks them to watch that patch through a gust and a lull, notice whether its surface appears to shimmer, ripple or break apart, then find a neighboring patch that changes less. The sign adds: “Still air? Watch for a short while; ‘no change’ is a valid observation.” No touching, approaching plants or timing device is needed.

The mechanism is temporal attention: movement can reveal how many small leaves, stems or flower heads combine into a surface. Comparing moving and relatively still patches may make their different structures more apparent. What changes the outcome is watching one place over time, rather than searching across a view. This is a plausible mechanism, not an established benefit.

The location must offer visibly different responses to ordinary breezes from a seated position. Sheltered planting, distant features or consistently still weather could make this unsuitable. The experience is primarily visual, and its value will vary with weather and vision.

Two volunteers use the existing map to shortlist permitted locations and inspect them during their observation shifts. They choose a clear seated sightline with room to pause outside the circulation route. One weatherproof panel carries a large quick invitation, three short optional steps and an arrow toward an existing landmark. A borrowed stable freestanding support keeps costs to printing if available. Week one covers site selection, week two a full-size comprehension check and revision, and week three the pilot.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate the interaction with a plain factual sign about the same planting during comparable blocks, recording breeze conditions alongside anonymous counts of passersby, stops and dwell-time bands. In selected staffed blocks, ask the same optional question under both conditions: “What, if anything, did movement help you notice?” Retain only aggregate counts of concrete texture observations, without visitor details or recordings. First check whether seated readers can distinguish two patches responding differently during a breeze. Failure rejects the location. If usable breezes rarely occur, or responses concern motion without any texture detail, the mechanism has weak practical support. Report descriptive pilot signals only.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Find the Missing Texture
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
A freestanding sign shows a deliberately simplified line drawing of the garden view ahead. It includes the main planting masses and a recognizable fixed landmark, but leaves one clearly bounded planting area blank. The invitation reads: “Ten seconds? What pattern belongs in the empty patch?” An optional two-minute sequence asks visitors to locate that patch in the real garden, imagine filling the blank with marks that represent its texture, and look for one feature the simplified drawing leaves out elsewhere. Nothing is drawn, submitted or collected.

The mechanism is completing an incomplete representation. The conspicuous blank creates a specific information gap; resolving it requires consulting the actual garden. Moving between a simplified picture and the living scene could make surface detail relevant in a way that an ordinary view does not. Unlike a sequence of viewing scales, the task turns on noticing what a representation omits.

This assumes the drawing is immediately recognizable from the sign, including from seated height, and that the missing patch contains visible texture. A confusing perspective would turn the activity into a navigation puzzle. Artistic confidence is unnecessary: the wording accepts imagined dots, strokes or any other marks. The interaction remains primarily visual and depends on adequate contrast and sightlines.

Two volunteers use the existing map to choose a permitted position, then make a basic outline drawing from the actual seated viewpoint. No specialist illustration is required; a few planting silhouettes and one fixed landmark suffice. A weatherproof panel and stable borrowed freestanding support are the only physical needs. During three weeks, they select and sketch the view, check a full-size prototype, revise it, and run observation shifts. Seasonal growth may require a later drawing update.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: First ask a few willing readers at seated height to locate the blank patch without coaching. Repeated wrong matches falsify the current drawing. Then alternate the panel with a plain information sign about the same view in comparable observation blocks. Tally anonymous traffic, stops and dwell-time bands. In selected staffed blocks, ask both groups: “What surface detail stood out?” Keep only aggregate counts of concrete texture descriptions, without personal details or recordings. If visitors solve the location puzzle but offer no texture observations, or descriptions are no more specific than with the comparator, the proposed benefit remains unsupported. Treat longer stops as engagement signals, not proof of noticing.

EXPAND.title: Wait for the Texture to Move
EXPAND.proposal:
The sign invites a short watch of one clearly indicated patch: “Ten seconds? Look for a texture that moves.” An optional two-minute sequence asks visitors to watch through a pause, notice which elements move together and which move separately, then consider how that movement changes the visible surface. A still-weather instruction says: “Nothing moving? Notice the texture holding its shape; try again another day.” All participation happens visually from the sign, without touching plants or approaching them.

The primary mechanism is temporal attention: movement can reveal overlapping layers, flexible stems and differences between loose and compact growth that a glance might miss. What changes the experience is watching one patch continuously instead of scanning several features. This assumes occasional visible movement and a patch whose structure remains legible from seated height. Wind is uncertain, and excessive movement could obscure detail; the still-weather version offers a brief observation but does not deliver the full mechanism.

Two volunteers use the existing map to shortlist permitted locations, then inspect actual views from seated height. Choose a patch with visible grasses, leaves or other moving elements, an unmistakable existing landmark, and safe stopping space. One weatherproof printed panel carries the quick invitation, optional sequence and still-weather fallback in large, high-contrast type. A stable freestanding support is required. Week one covers siting and drafting; week two covers readability and a seated prototype check; week three covers observation shifts and the pilot. No visitor equipment or physical response is needed.
EXPAND.experiment: Alternate the interaction and a plain information panel about the same patch on the same support. Counterbalance their order across comparable observation blocks and note broad wind conditions. Tally anonymous passersby, stops and dwell bands. In optional verbal checks, ask what moving features revealed about the surface; retain only aggregate counts of texture-specific responses, without visitor details or recordings. The mechanism is weakened if seated readers cannot see differential movement, repeatedly need explanation, or offer no more texture-specific observations than comparator readers under similar conditions. Report feasibility and descriptive differences only; weather imbalance may prevent a useful comparison.

EXPAND.title: Look Away, Then Check
EXPAND.proposal:
A freestanding sign offers a small memory challenge: “Ten seconds? Look at this patch, look away, then check one detail you missed.” The optional two-minute version asks visitors to study the indicated planting briefly, turn their gaze to a blank printed rectangle on the sign, recall its visible surface, and look back for a feature absent from that recollection. They can repeat once, then finish by choosing one newly noticed detail. Nobody needs to close their eyes, change position, write, speak or touch anything.

The primary mechanism is a mismatch between remembered appearance and renewed observation. A familiar planting may initially register as a general mass; trying to recall its texture creates a specific reason to inspect it again. The working assumption is that some visible structure will be omitted from a brief recollection. This is uncertain and should be tested. Memory effort can also be frustrating, so the sign explicitly permits skipping recall and simply taking a second look. That fallback is accessible but does not test the proposed mechanism.

Two volunteers select a permitted position using the map and a seated-height inspection. The indicated patch must have visible surface variation without requiring small details or a distant view. Print a large, high-contrast three-step sequence and an unpatterned resting area on one weatherproof panel. An existing landmark identifies the patch. A stable freestanding support and clear stopping space are the only other needs. Draft and site the panel in week one, inspect a full-size prototype in week two, and revise and pilot in week three. The activity remains primarily visual and may not suit every visitor.
EXPAND.experiment: Alternate with a plain information sign describing the same view, using the same support and comparable blocks with order reversed across shifts. Count passersby, stops and dwell bands anonymously. During selected staffed blocks, offer one optional question: “Did looking again reveal a surface detail you had missed?” Count only responses that include a concrete visible example, without retaining quotations or visitor details. First check that seated readers understand the look-away step without coaching. Frequent confusion, discomfort, or no clearer examples than the comparator would weaken the proposal. Self-reports cannot establish that a detail was previously unnoticed; report them as limited pilot signals.

EXPAND.title: Look Through the Gaps
EXPAND.proposal:
The sign redirects attention to the spaces within one visible planting: “Ten seconds? Find a gap you can see through.” The optional two-minute interaction asks visitors to keep looking at that same patch while attending first to the leaves or stems, then to the openings between them. They notice whether those openings form a continuous mesh, scattered holes or narrow channels, and finish by viewing the whole surface again. These descriptions explain the task; visitors do not have to choose a label or find a correct answer.

The primary mechanism is a reversal of figure and background. Attending to empty spaces can make the density, layering and porosity of a plant surface more apparent. What changes is which part of the same view receives attention, without changing scale or asking visitors to imagine drawing. It depends on a planting with visible internal gaps and a sufficiently contrasting background. Dense foliage, a cluttered background or seasonal growth could make the reversal ineffective. The sign should therefore identify a verified patch rather than invite an unrestricted search.

Two volunteers consult the existing map, inspect candidate views from seated height, and choose a permitted location with a clear landmark and room to stop. A single weatherproof panel uses large text and a simple generic illustration of filled shapes and the spaces between them. The illustration teaches where to look without pretending to reproduce the planting. All viewing remains possible from one position; no touching, writing, phone or power is involved. Preparation takes three weeks: siting and drafting, full-size seated readability checks and revision, then the pilot. Material needs are printing and a stable freestanding support. Passing visitors can complete the first observation immediately.
EXPAND.experiment: Use alternating, counterbalanced observation blocks against a plain information sign about the same planting. Volunteers record anonymous passing counts, stops and dwell bands, plus whether the target remains clearly visible. In optional verbal checks, ask readers to indicate a gap and describe what its arrangement reveals about the surrounding surface; retain aggregate completion counts only. The smallest falsifying check is whether seated readers can distinguish the openings without moving or receiving explanation. If they cannot, reject the location. If they find gaps but describe no surface structure, the proposed connection to texture needs revision. Comparator differences remain exploratory, with no claim of demonstrated benefit.

EXPAND.title: Find the Pattern’s Garden Twin
EXPAND.proposal:
A freestanding sign displays three large, abstract black-and-white patterns: overlapping scales, irregular speckles and parallel ridges. Its quick invitation reads: “Ten seconds? Find a garden surface that resembles one of these patterns.” The optional two-minute interaction continues: choose one pattern, find its closest visible match in the indicated garden view, then inspect where the living surface differs from the printed pattern. Finish by noticing one irregularity the print cannot capture. There is no correct match, and all searching happens from the sign without touching plants.

The mechanism is visual template matching: a simple printed pattern gives attention a specific structure to seek within otherwise undifferentiated planting. Comparing the match with its simplified template may then reveal variation, such as uneven spacing or overlapping layers. The outcome depends on the patterns directing attention toward actual visible textures; attractive graphics alone would not establish that.

Two volunteers use the existing map to shortlist permitted positions, then inspect views from seated height. Select a clear view with at least two plausible pattern matches visible without moving closer. Use large, high-contrast graphics, concise instructions and an existing landmark to identify the search area. The activity remains primarily visual and may offer limited access for some visitors with low vision.

Week one covers siting and pattern selection; week two covers a full-size seated readability check and revision; week three covers the pilot. Materials are one weatherproof printed panel and a stable freestanding support, positioned clear of circulation. No equipment or response materials are needed from visitors.
EXPAND.experiment: Alternate the activity panel with a plain garden information panel on the same support during comparable observation shifts. Volunteers record only anonymous aggregate counts of passersby, stops and visible turns toward the indicated planting; these cannot establish texture noticing. For a small direct check, invite a few willing visitors in each condition to point out a texture they noticed, without requesting or recording personal details. Note whether their examples identify visible surface structure. Revise or reject the design if seated users cannot locate plausible matches, graphics cause confusion, or activity users chiefly describe the printed patterns rather than the garden. Treat any differences as exploratory, not demonstrated effects.

In a small number of staffed checks, invite visitors to name one visible feature supporting their chosen word; keep only aggregate counts, without collecting identifying information or recording speech. Include readers viewing from seated height in the prototype check. The central challenge is whether the words cause closer inspection: if people choose immediately but cannot point out any supporting feature, or describe no more texture detail than readers of the plain sign, the proposed mechanism has weak support. Also check whether either word is consistently confusing. Treat findings as local pilot signals, not demonstrated benefits.

REFINE.title: Draw It in the Air—with Your Eyes
REFINE.proposal:
A freestanding sign invites visitors to imagine drawing one visible garden texture without moving their hands: “Ten seconds? Follow one edge with your eyes.” The optional two-minute sequence continues: trace a second edge, notice whether its imagined line would be straight, broken, curling or branching, then find a nearby texture that would need a different kind of line. Visitors finish by looking back at the original patch.

The mechanism is imagined mark-making. Translating a surface into lines may shift attention from identifying plants to noticing the structure of their edges, veins, stems and shadows. It is independently usable without drawing supplies, touching plants, power or a phone. The assumption is that visitors can distinguish sufficiently large contours from the sign. Some people find mental imagery difficult, so the wording also permits simply following an outline and comparing its shape. It remains primarily a visual experience and will have limits for visitors with low vision.

Two volunteers use the garden map and a seated-height inspection to choose a permitted position facing clear, contrasting outlines. A weatherproof panel carries three large example strokes and concise instructions; the examples explain the action without purporting to depict every plant. The sign directs attention using an unmistakable landmark already in the view. A stable freestanding support sits outside the circulation route. Preparation fits three weeks: choose the view and draft in week one, test readability and landmark clarity in week two, then revise and pilot in week three. Printing and the support are the only material needs. Avoid tiny veins or distant features that would encourage visitors to leave the accessible viewing point.
REFINE.experiment: Alternate the interaction with a plain information sign about the same garden view, using comparable time blocks and the same support. Volunteers tally passing traffic, stops and dwell-time bands anonymously. A few optional verbal checks ask visitors to identify two textures that would require different drawing strokes; record only aggregate completion counts, with no identifying details or recordings. Before the pilot, test whether seated readers can find the landmark and follow a contour without changing position. The idea is weakened if instructions repeatedly require explanation, readers cannot identify contrasting strokes, or the plain information sign elicits equally specific texture distinctions. Observe across more than one light condition because shadows may determine legibility. Report feasibility and descriptive differences only; this small pilot cannot establish a reliable effect.

REFINE.title: Look Through the Gaps
REFINE.proposal:
A freestanding sign invites visitors to notice texture by looking at the empty spaces within a planting: “Ten seconds? Find one gap between leaves or stems. Notice its shape.” The optional two-minute interaction continues: find several neighboring gaps, notice how their spacing creates a loose or dense pattern, then look back at the plants surrounding them. Everything happens from the sign; visitors need not approach or touch plants.

The mechanism is figure–ground reversal. Attention normally falls on plants as objects; treating the background openings as the subject may expose the arrangement that makes foliage appear lacy, mesh-like or tightly packed. The change in attention, rather than a change in viewing scale or a choice of descriptive words, drives the interaction.

This requires a planting with clearly visible openings against a contrasting background from seated height. Dense foliage, poor contrast or seasonal growth could make the exercise ineffective. It is primarily visual and cannot offer equivalent access to every visitor.

Two volunteers use the existing map to shortlist permitted locations, then inspect the actual sightlines from seated height. One weatherproof panel uses large, high-contrast text, an arrow toward an existing landmark and a simple illustration of spaces between shapes. A stable freestanding support must fit the available budget or be borrowed, and leave circulation clear. Week one covers siting and drafting; week two covers a full-size readability and seated-view check; week three covers revision and observation shifts. There are no loose pieces, writing tasks or visitor records.
REFINE.experiment: Alternate the interaction and a plain information sign about the same planting in comparable observation blocks on the same support. Tally anonymous passing traffic, stops and approximate dwell-time bands. During selected staffed blocks, ask an optional question: “What pattern, if any, did you notice?” Keep only aggregate counts of responses describing gaps, spacing or plant texture, without names, recordings or visitor characteristics. The smallest falsifying check is whether a seated reader can identify several visible gaps without explanation or repositioning. If that fails, reject the location. If readers notice isolated holes but cannot relate them to the surrounding texture, or responses are no more specific than with the information sign, the proposed mechanism has weak support. Report local descriptive signals only.

REFINE.title: Look Away, Then Look Again
REFINE.proposal:
A freestanding sign offers a brief visual-memory challenge: “Ten seconds? Look at this planting, look away briefly, then look back. What detail escaped your first look?” The optional two-minute version asks visitors to study a clearly indicated patch, turn their gaze toward a printed dot on the sign, silently recall its surface pattern, then return to the patch and find something missing from their mental picture. They may repeat once, keeping their gaze shifts comfortable and their head still.

The mechanism is a gap between remembered appearance and visible detail. A planting may initially register as a general mass; attempting to recall its texture can make missing information apparent and give the second look a specific purpose. Success means discovering a previously omitted feature, rather than remembering accurately. No answer is written or submitted.

This assumes visitors can comfortably alternate their gaze between sign and planting and understand the short sequence. Visual memory varies, and some people may find the challenge frustrating. The sign therefore says that an incomplete memory is expected and that participation can end after one return look. The experience remains primarily visual.

Two volunteers use the garden map and seated-height inspections to select a clear, nearby view with visible texture and an unmistakable landmark. They produce one weatherproof panel with large text and three simple symbols: look, look away, return. The panel sits on a stable permitted freestanding support outside the circulation route. Printing and a borrowed or inexpensive support are the material needs. Within three weeks, the volunteers select the site, check a full-size prototype for readability and comprehension, revise it, and run observation shifts.
REFINE.experiment: Compare this panel with a plain information sign about the same view, alternating comparable observation blocks. Volunteers tally anonymous passersby, stops and dwell-time bands. In a few staffed blocks, offer the same optional question under both conditions: “Did a second look reveal any texture detail you missed initially?” Retain only aggregate counts of concrete examples, with no identifying information or recordings. First conduct a small seated-position comprehension check: can readers complete the sequence without coaching? Repeated confusion, discomfort or interpreting it as a memory exam would falsify the current wording. If the sequence is understood but yields no more concrete discoveries than the plain sign, its added value remains unsupported. Dwell time alone cannot establish noticing; report the pilot descriptively without claiming effectiveness.

REFINE.title: Look Through the Gaps: Compare Two Clusters
REFINE.proposal:
Repair of original candidate 3, the strongest fit for its simple, equipment-free shift of attention. Exact weakness: finding an isolated gap can reveal a hole without helping visitors notice the texture created by repeated spaces. Change the longer sequence to compare the gaps within two adjacent foliage clusters, identified by existing landmarks: “Ten seconds? Find a space between leaves in this cluster. Staying seated? Everything is visible from here. Have two minutes? Look at several neighboring spaces, then those in the other cluster. Where are the spaces more tightly packed? Look back at the leaves: how do those spaces shape the texture?” This preserves figure–ground reversal while making the relationship between gaps and texture concrete.

Prerequisite: both clusters must show repeated openings with visibly different spacing from the same seated viewing position; use the existing map to shortlist locations and inspect them directly. Two volunteers spend week one selecting the view, week two checking and revising a full-size panel, and week three piloting it. Use large, high-contrast weatherproof print on one borrowed, stable freestanding support, positioned for seated reading without blocking circulation. No touching, additional fixtures, power, phone or visitor details are needed. Remaining limit: growth, lighting and visual acuity can make the spacing contrast inaccessible.
REFINE.experiment: Smallest falsifying prototype: from seated height, each volunteer independently follows the full-size draft and identifies repeated gaps in both clusters without moving closer. If either cluster reads only as an undifferentiated mass, reject that location. Pilot against a plain factual information panel about the same planting on the same support, using comparable typography and length. Alternate equal observation blocks and reverse their order across shifts. Tally anonymous passersby, stops and dwell-time bands. During selected staffed blocks, ask the same optional question in both conditions: “What texture or pattern, if any, stood out?” Retain only aggregate counts of concrete descriptions, including whether they connect spacing to foliage texture; collect no visitor details or verbatim responses. Stops alone do not demonstrate noticing. If descriptions remain limited to isolated holes, or are no more specific than under the plain sign, the repair has little support. Report descriptive pilot signals only; no results are claimed.

SAVE.title: One View, Three Scales
SAVE.proposal:
A freestanding sign guides an optional two-minute visual search within one garden view: “Ten seconds? Find one texture you had not noticed.” The longer sequence asks visitors to look across the whole planting for a soft or jagged outline, choose one visible patch with repeated marks, then look for the smallest detail they can comfortably distinguish. Finish by returning to the whole view and noticing whether it now looks different. No approach to plants is required.

The mechanism is a deliberate change in viewing scale: successive prompts may interrupt habitual scanning and reveal texture already present. This assumes the permitted sign location offers several distinguishable textures from a seated position. Fine detail may be inaccessible to some visitors, so each step explicitly allows staying with larger patterns; the interaction does not promise equal visual access.

Two volunteers use the existing map to shortlist locations, then inspect actual views from seated height. Choose one with clear sightlines and room to stop without obstructing circulation. Print three large, high-contrast prompts on weatherproof material, with a simple diagram showing the relevant viewing direction. Keep the quick invitation prominent and the longer sequence optional. Week one covers siting and drafting, week two a full-size readability check and revision, and week three the pilot. Costs are printing and a permitted, stable sign support; no additional installation is needed.
SAVE.experiment: Alternate this sign and a plain information sign on the same support in comparable observation blocks. The comparator gives factual information about the same visible planting, with similar print size and text length. Volunteers tally anonymous passersby, stops, approximate dwell-time bands, and visible shifts between the indicated garden areas; gaze alone cannot establish noticing. During a few staffed blocks, offer an optional verbal question: “What texture, if any, stood out?” Record only aggregate counts of specific texture descriptions, without names, recordings or visitor characteristics. A small falsifying check is whether seated readers can locate the three scales at all. If they cannot, or interaction blocks produce no clearer texture descriptions than the comparator, revise or drop the sequence. Report the small pilot descriptively, without claiming effectiveness.

SAVE.title: Which Word Fits?
SAVE.proposal:
A freestanding sign presents three short pairs of contrasting texture words, such as “rippled / tangled,” “velvety / wiry,” and “layered / scattered.” Visitors silently choose which word best describes one clearly indicated garden patch. The ten-second version is one choice; the optional two-minute version asks them to find evidence for both words, then invent a better description in their head. The sign says that these are visual comparisons, not invitations to touch.

The mechanism is interpretive disagreement: choosing between imperfect labels gives visitors a reason to inspect a familiar-looking surface more carefully. Seeking evidence for the rejected word can expose overlooked variation. Unlike a factual identification exercise, there is no correct answer to reveal. Its value depends on the chosen patch supporting more than one plausible description; a visually uniform or obscured patch would make the choice arbitrary.

Using the existing map, two volunteers select a permitted sign position beside a view containing visibly contrasting textures at seated eye level. They draft everyday words and simple line illustrations so the invitation does not depend entirely on vocabulary. Large type, strong contrast and an unobstructed stopping space support seated participation. Visitors may complete everything silently, without writing, tokens or moving components. One weatherproof printed panel and stable freestanding support suffice. Across three weeks, the volunteers inspect the location, check the language and seated sightline, revise the print, and run observation shifts. Seasonal changes and unfamiliar metaphorical words remain limitations; labels must be chosen for the actual view.
SAVE.experiment: Pilot against a plain information sign describing the same patch, alternating matched observation blocks at the same location. Count anonymous passersby, stops and dwell-time bands. In a small number of staffed checks, invite visitors to name one visible feature supporting their chosen word; keep only aggregate counts, without collecting identifying information or recording speech. Include readers viewing from seated height in the prototype check. The central challenge is whether the words cause closer inspection: if people choose immediately but cannot point out any supporting feature, or describe no more texture detail than readers of the plain sign, the proposed mechanism has weak support. Also check whether either word is consistently confusing. Treat findings as local pilot signals, not demonstrated benefits.

SAVE.title: Wait for the Texture to Move
SAVE.proposal:
The sign invites a short watch of one clearly indicated patch: “Ten seconds? Look for a texture that moves.” An optional two-minute sequence asks visitors to watch through a pause, notice which elements move together and which move separately, then consider how that movement changes the visible surface. A still-weather instruction says: “Nothing moving? Notice the texture holding its shape; try again another day.” All participation happens visually from the sign, without touching plants or approaching them.

The primary mechanism is temporal attention: movement can reveal overlapping layers, flexible stems and differences between loose and compact growth that a glance might miss. What changes the experience is watching one patch continuously instead of scanning several features. This assumes occasional visible movement and a patch whose structure remains legible from seated height. Wind is uncertain, and excessive movement could obscure detail; the still-weather version offers a brief observation but does not deliver the full mechanism.

Two volunteers use the existing map to shortlist permitted locations, then inspect actual views from seated height. Choose a patch with visible grasses, leaves or other moving elements, an unmistakable existing landmark, and safe stopping space. One weatherproof printed panel carries the quick invitation, optional sequence and still-weather fallback in large, high-contrast type. A stable freestanding support is required. Week one covers siting and drafting; week two covers readability and a seated prototype check; week three covers observation shifts and the pilot. No visitor equipment or physical response is needed.
SAVE.experiment: Alternate the interaction and a plain information panel about the same patch on the same support. Counterbalance their order across comparable observation blocks and note broad wind conditions. Tally anonymous passersby, stops and dwell bands. In optional verbal checks, ask what moving features revealed about the surface; retain only aggregate counts of texture-specific responses, without visitor details or recordings. The mechanism is weakened if seated readers cannot see differential movement, repeatedly need explanation, or offer no more texture-specific observations than comparator readers under similar conditions. Report feasibility and descriptive differences only; weather imbalance may prevent a useful comparison.

SAVE.title: Look Away, Then Check
SAVE.proposal:
A freestanding sign offers a small memory challenge: “Ten seconds? Look at this patch, look away, then check one detail you missed.” The optional two-minute version asks visitors to study the indicated planting briefly, turn their gaze to a blank printed rectangle on the sign, recall its visible surface, and look back for a feature absent from that recollection. They can repeat once, then finish by choosing one newly noticed detail. Nobody needs to close their eyes, change position, write, speak or touch anything.

The primary mechanism is a mismatch between remembered appearance and renewed observation. A familiar planting may initially register as a general mass; trying to recall its texture creates a specific reason to inspect it again. The working assumption is that some visible structure will be omitted from a brief recollection. This is uncertain and should be tested. Memory effort can also be frustrating, so the sign explicitly permits skipping recall and simply taking a second look. That fallback is accessible but does not test the proposed mechanism.

Two volunteers select a permitted position using the map and a seated-height inspection. The indicated patch must have visible surface variation without requiring small details or a distant view. Print a large, high-contrast three-step sequence and an unpatterned resting area on one weatherproof panel. An existing landmark identifies the patch. A stable freestanding support and clear stopping space are the only other needs. Draft and site the panel in week one, inspect a full-size prototype in week two, and revise and pilot in week three. The activity remains primarily visual and may not suit every visitor.
SAVE.experiment: Alternate with a plain information sign describing the same view, using the same support and comparable blocks with order reversed across shifts. Count passersby, stops and dwell bands anonymously. During selected staffed blocks, offer one optional question: “Did looking again reveal a surface detail you had missed?” Count only responses that include a concrete visible example, without retaining quotations or visitor details. First check that seated readers understand the look-away step without coaching. Frequent confusion, discomfort, or no clearer examples than the comparator would weaken the proposal. Self-reports cannot establish that a detail was previously unnoticed; report them as limited pilot signals.

SAVE.title: Look Through the Gaps
SAVE.proposal:
The sign redirects attention to the spaces within one visible planting: “Ten seconds? Find a gap you can see through.” The optional two-minute interaction asks visitors to keep looking at that same patch while attending first to the leaves or stems, then to the openings between them. They notice whether those openings form a continuous mesh, scattered holes or narrow channels, and finish by viewing the whole surface again. These descriptions explain the task; visitors do not have to choose a label or find a correct answer.

The primary mechanism is a reversal of figure and background. Attending to empty spaces can make the density, layering and porosity of a plant surface more apparent. What changes is which part of the same view receives attention, without changing scale or asking visitors to imagine drawing. It depends on a planting with visible internal gaps and a sufficiently contrasting background. Dense foliage, a cluttered background or seasonal growth could make the reversal ineffective. The sign should therefore identify a verified patch rather than invite an unrestricted search.

Two volunteers consult the existing map, inspect candidate views from seated height, and choose a permitted location with a clear landmark and room to stop. A single weatherproof panel uses large text and a simple generic illustration of filled shapes and the spaces between them. The illustration teaches where to look without pretending to reproduce the planting. All viewing remains possible from one position; no touching, writing, phone or power is involved. Preparation takes three weeks: siting and drafting, full-size seated readability checks and revision, then the pilot. Material needs are printing and a stable freestanding support. Passing visitors can complete the first observation immediately.
SAVE.experiment: Use alternating, counterbalanced observation blocks against a plain information sign about the same planting. Volunteers record anonymous passing counts, stops and dwell bands, plus whether the target remains clearly visible. In optional verbal checks, ask readers to indicate a gap and describe what its arrangement reveals about the surrounding surface; retain aggregate completion counts only. The smallest falsifying check is whether seated readers can distinguish the openings without moving or receiving explanation. If they cannot, reject the location. If they find gaps but describe no surface structure, the proposed connection to texture needs revision. Comparator differences remain exploratory, with no claim of demonstrated benefit.
